newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lead dwindles in Reuters tracking poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lead dwindles in Reuters tracking poll.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
Republican Bob Dole has cut President Clinton's lead in the presidential race to only 5.5 percentage points, according to the latest Reuters daily tracking poll issued Friday.

Clinton led with 42 percent, ahead of Dole's 36.5 percent in the poll of 1,200 likely voters conducted Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday by John Zogby Group International. Election Day is next Tuesday, Nov 5.
Reform Party candidate Ross Perot scored 8.4 percent and 11.2 percent remained undecided in the survey, which has a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points.
Pollster John Zogby said that Clinton's lead in Thursday's polling alone was only 3.5 points, but because that was a smaller sample, it carried a larger margin of error.
"Something is clearly happening out there. The number of undecided voters, which was growing earlier this week, dropped dramatically in Thursday's polling and most of those went to Dole," he said.
In Thursday polling, the undecided vote was down to 6.4 percent, from 15.3 percent earlier in the week.
The poll showed Dole building a lead over Clinton among Protestants, among those who have lost a job in the past year, and among those who live in households earning $75,000 a year or more.
He was also cutting Clinton's advantage in the Midwest and Great Lakes region, in states where he must do well to have any chance next Tuesday.
U.S. elections are actually 51 separate contests in each of the 50 states and the District of Columbia for delegates to the Electoral College, where 270 votes are needed for victory.

Zogby said state by state polling appeared to indicate Clinton remained in a solid position to win the election, although there were some signs the race was tightening. A new poll in Georgia Friday showed a previously wide Clinton lead had evaporated and the state was now too close to call.

Clinton's lead in the Reuters poll stood at 13 percentage points only five days ago. Since then however, he has withstood a battering from Dole and Perot over the issue of campaign finance, fuelled by a stream of media reports about the activities of John Huang, a Democratic fundraiser and former Commerce Department official who collected large sums from Asian subsidiaries.
After ignoring the issue for days, Clinton planned to address it in a speech in California Friday.

The Washington Post and New York Times report that John Huang, who was suspended from his Democratic Party fundraising duties two weeks ago amid reports that he unlawfully solicited foreign contributions, had made at least 78 visits to the White House since July 1, 1995.
The race for Congress remains extremely close, with the Democrats holding a slight edge of 39.3 percent to 37.8 percent when voters were asked who they would support in their own districts.
However, when asked which party they would prefer to see controlling Congress, voters preferred Republicans in the Senate by a margin of six points and in the House by a margin of five points.
